chief_complaint: sharp shooting pain down my right arm into my middle finger and weak triceps for 3 weeks
hpi_details: 3-week history of sharp, burning, electric shock-like pain radiating from the right side of her neck across the shoulder and down the back of her right arm into the middle and index fingers. Pain is worsened by extending her neck backward or turning her head to the right. Accompanied by pins-and-needles numbness in the index and middle fingers, and noticed significant weakness when doing push-ups or trying to extend her right arm against resistance at the gym. Symptoms started suddenly after heavy overhead lifting while renovating her kitchen. Denies leg weakness, gait clumsiness, or bladder/bowel disturbances.
ideas: thinks he tore a muscle or rotator cuff tendon in his right shoulder during kitchen renovations
concerns: worried he will lose the strength in his right arm permanently and be unable to work as a carpenter
expectations: wants shoulder physiotherapy and a cortisone joint injection into the shoulder to relieve the shooting pain
pmh: mild chronic lower back pain, no prior neck or nerve surgery
medications: ibuprofen 400mg TDS and paracetamol with moderate relief
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks socially, self-employed carpenter, right-hand dominant

clinical_knowledge.topic: C7 Cervical Radiculopathy evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of C7 Cervical Radiculopathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Most cases resolve without surgery within 6 to 12 weeks; management includes appropriate analgesia, activity modification, and physiotherapy, with escalation for progressive neurological deficit.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp shooting pain down my right arm into my middle finger and weak triceps for 3 weeks

Key HPI features: 3-week history of sharp, burning, electric shock-like pain radiating from the right side of his neck across the shoulder and down the back of his right arm into the middle and index fingers. Pain is worsened by extending his neck backward or turning his head to the right. Accompanied by pins-and-needles numbness in the index and middle fingers, and noticed significant weakness when doing push-ups or trying to extend his right arm against resistance at the gym. Symptoms started suddenly after heavy overhead lifting while renovating his kitchen. Denies leg weakness, gait clumsiness, or bladder/bowel disturbances.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform cervical spine and upper limb neurological exam: Spurling's test positive on the right (neck extension and lateral flexion to the right reproduces shooting radicular pain down the right arm). Motor exam: weakness in right elbow extension (triceps power 4/5) and right wrist flexion (myotome C7). Sensory exam: pinprick and light touch reduced over the dorsum of the right middle finger (dermatome C7). Reflexes: diminished right triceps jerk (C7 reflex) with preserved biceps and brachioradialis reflexes. CRITICAL SCREENING: test lower limb tone, power, Babinski reflex, and Hoffman's sign to rule out Cervical Myelopathy (spinal cord compression). MRI Cervical Spine without contrast: confirms right posterolateral C6-C7 intervertebral disc herniation compressing the exiting right C7 nerve root in the neural foramen.
Relevant background/PMH: mild chronic lower back pain, no prior neck or nerve surgery
Current medications: ibuprofen 400mg TDS and paracetamol with moderate relief
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out C7 Cervical Radiculopathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rotator cuff tear/shoulder pathology without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Leg weakness, gait problems, or bladder/bowel changes — would suggest spinal cord (myelopathy) involvement instead.
management_principles: Formulate a conservative management plan: appropriate analgesia, activity modification, and physiotherapy; consider neuropathic analgesia when clinically appropriate.
Refer to specialized musculoskeletal physiotherapy for gentle cervical traction and postural stabilization
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 47F carpenter presents with right C7 radicular pain, dermatomal numbness (middle/index fingers), and myotomal weakness (triceps) post-overhead lifting. No myelopathy or red flags.
reference_soap.objective: Perform cervical spine and upper limb neurological exam: Spurling's test positive on the right (neck extension and lateral flexion to the right reproduces shooting radicular pain down the right arm). Motor exam: weakness in right elbow extension (triceps power 4/5) and right wrist flexion (myotome C7). Sensory exam: pinprick and light touch reduced over the dorsum of the right middle finger (dermatome C7). Reflexes: diminished right triceps jerk (C7 reflex) with preserved biceps and brachioradialis reflexes. CRITICAL SCREENING: test lower limb tone, power, Babinski reflex, and Hoffman's sign to rule out Cervical Myelopathy (spinal cord compression). MRI Cervical Spine without contrast: confirms right posterolateral C6-C7 intervertebral disc herniation compressing the exiting right C7 nerve root in the neural foramen.
reference_soap.assessment: Right C7 Cervical Radiculopathy secondary to C6-C7 posterolateral disc herniation. DDx: rotator cuff tear / shoulder pathology (ruled out by positive Spurling's and neurological deficits), peripheral nerve entrapment (carpal/cubital tunnel syndrome), brachial neuritis (Parsonage-Turner syndrome), cervical spondylotic myelopathy.
reference_soap.plan: Formulate conservative management plan (>80% resolve without surgery within 6 to 12 weeks): short course of oral NSAIDs plus neuropathic analgesia (e.g., pregabalin starting 50mg BID or amitriptyline 10mg ON). Refer to specialized musculoskeletal physiotherapy for gentle cervical traction and postural stabilization. Advise to avoid overhead heavy lifting and extreme neck extension. Outpatient neurosurgery/orthopaedic spine referral for consideration of fluoroscopic cervical transforaminal epidural steroid injection or anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) if motor weakness progresses or debilitating pain persists beyond 8-12 weeks.

learning_objectives: Map clinical findings precisely to the C7 nerve root distribution (pain down dorsum of arm, middle finger numbness, triceps weakness and reflex loss)
Perform and interpret Spurling's foraminal compression test while systematically excluding cervical myelopathy signs (Babinski, Hoffman's)
Differentiate cervical radiculopathy from intrinsic shoulder joint pathology using dermatomal/myotomal localization
Outline the evidence-based conservative trajectory (>80% resolution) and specific triggers for neurosurgical escalation

teaching.one_liner: A herniated disc in the neck compresses the C7 nerve root, causing electric shock-like pain radiating down the arm into the middle finger, weakness extending the arm (triceps), and numbness — most resolve without surgery within weeks.
red_flags: Leg weakness, gait problems, or bladder/bowel changes — would suggest spinal cord (myelopathy) involvement instead

must_ask.say: Does the pain go from your neck down your arm into a specific finger?
Does turning your head or tilting it back make the pain worse?
Did this start after heavy lifting or overhead work?
Have you noticed weakness pushing or extending your arm?
Any weakness in your legs or changes in bladder/bowel control?

history.answer: My right arm has been having sharp, shooting pains and tingling down into my middle finger, and my arm feels weak.
It feels like a sharp, burning, electric shock that shoots from the right side of my neck across my shoulder and down the back of my arm into my index and middle fingers.
I have both pins-and-needles numbness in my middle and index fingers, and actual weakness when I try to push or straighten my right arm.
It started abruptly three weeks ago while I was lifting heavy kitchen cabinets overhead during a renovation.
The pain and weakness have stayed constant and intense ever since it started, without really getting better.
Tipping my head backward or turning my head to the right makes the electric shock shoot right down my arm.
Resting my neck and taking ibuprofen takes the edge off slightly, but raising my arm overhead or extending my neck brings it right back.
I noticed severe weakness when trying to do push-ups at the gym and pushing heavy planks at work, though I can still button my shirt and hold cups.
I have an aching stiffness on the right side of my neck where the shock begins, and I also have an old mild ache in my lower back, but no sharp leg pain.
No, my legs feel completely normal and strong, and my walking is steady without any stumbling.
No, my bowel and bladder habits are completely normal, and I have normal feeling around my groin and bottom.
No, I haven't had any slurred speech, facial drooping, double vision, or trouble swallowing.
No shortness of breath, drooping eyelids, or trouble chewing.
No, I haven't noticed any muscle twitches or shrinking in my arm muscles.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, stomach flu, or recent viral illness.
I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart rhythm problems.
I eat a balanced diet with plenty of meat and vegetables, and I have never had stomach surgery.
I haven't taken any steroids, water pills, or nerve medications.
As a carpenter, I do lots of repetitive sawing, hammering, and overhead lifting, but I don't rest on my elbows or sit curled up for long periods.
I thought I might have torn a muscle or a rotator cuff tendon in my right shoulder while lifting those heavy cabinets.
I am really worried that this weakness in my right arm might be permanent and keep me from working as a carpenter.
I was hoping I could get shoulder physiotherapy and maybe a cortisone injection into my shoulder joint to stop this pain.
Aside from mild chronic lower back pain, I have no other medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take ibuprofen 400 milligrams three times a day and paracetamol as needed, which gives some mild relief.
I do not have any allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I drink socially, maybe two or three beers on the weekend.
I am self-employed as a carpenter and live at home with my partner.
There is no family history of nerve disorders, stroke, or muscle diseases.
My last period was about two weeks ago; my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, I use barrier contraception, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Symmetric facial movements, intact extraocular movements without nystagmus, normal speech, and no visual field cuts.

Spurling test is positive on the right, reproducing sharp shooting pain down the right arm into the middle finger; cervical paraspinal tightness without midline bony tenderness, and negative straight-leg raise bilaterally.
Full active and passive range of motion in both shoulders, elbows, and wrists without local joint tenderness, swelling, or impingement signs.

Right elbow extension (triceps) and right wrist flexion are 4/5; right deltoid, biceps, and intrinsic hand muscles are 5/5, and left upper limb and both lower limbs are 5/5 without fasciculations or atrophy.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the dorsum of the right middle finger (C7 dermatome); sensation is intact in other upper limb dermatomes and both lower extremities.

Right triceps reflex is 1+ (diminished); right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are 2+, all left upper limb and bilateral lower extremity reflexes are 2+, and Babinski and Hoffman signs are negative.
Normal steady gait, normal tandem walk, and negative Romberg test.
